bhutan: A white dragon lies across a diagonal split of yellow and orange.
Its emblem clutches jewels in its claws.
One half represents royal authority and the other a Buddhist tradition.
The creature on it is also part of the country's name in its own language.
brazil: A yellow diamond on green, with a starry blue globe crossed by a white motto band.
Its stars show a real night sky from the morning a monarchy fell.
Its motto comes from a French philosopher's school of thought.
Its green and yellow came from the dynasties of an emperor and his Austrian wife.
canada: Red bars on either side of a white square containing a single red leaf.
Its leaf has eleven points, chosen after wind-tunnel testing.
A heraldic term for a central square as wide as the flag is tall is named after it.
It replaced a red ensign after a long parliamentary debate in 1964.
denmark: A white off-centre cross on a red field.
Legend says it fell from the sky during a battle in 1219.
Every other flag of its regional cross family is modelled on it.
Often called the oldest national flag still in continuous use.
france: A vertical tricolour with blue at the hoist and red at the fly.
The colours of its capital city were combined with the white of a royal dynasty during a revolution.
Its navy flies a version with unequal stripes so it looks even in the wind.
Decreed by a revolutionary assembly in 1794, it was banned for fifteen years after an emperor's fall.
germany: Three horizontal bands: black on top, then red, then gold.
Its colours trace back to the uniforms of a volunteer corps that fought Napoleon.
A revolutionary parliament adopted it in 1848, but it became official only in 1919.
For forty years two neighbouring states used it, one with a hammer and compass added.
india: Saffron, white and green horizontal stripes with a navy wheel in the middle.
Its central wheel has 24 spokes and comes from an emperor's stone pillar.
A spinning wheel was replaced by a wheel of law weeks before independence.
Its flag code once required the flag to be made from hand-spun cloth.
japan: A single red circle centred on a white field, nothing else.
Its disc used to sit very slightly toward the hoist until a 1999 law centred it.
The disc evokes a goddess from whom an imperial dynasty claims descent.
kenya: Black, red and green bands with thin white stripes, and a shield and two spears in the centre.
The shield on it is of a traditional pastoralist people's design.
Its colours come from the party that led the country to independence in 1963.
lebanon: A green tree on a white band between two red bands.
Its central tree touches both of the coloured bands.
Before independence its tree sat on a European tricolour.
mexico: Green, white and red vertical bands with an eagle eating a snake on a cactus.
Its emblem retells the founding legend of a city built on a lake.
Remove its emblem and it closely resembles a European flag.
Its current emblem was redrawn just before its capital hosted the Olympics.
mozambique: A red hoist triangle with a star, a book, a hoe and a rifle.
The only national flag that shows an assault rifle.
Green, black and yellow bands edged in white, inherited from a liberation movement.
nepal: The only national flag that is not a rectangle.
Two stacked crimson pennants with a blue border.
A white moon above and a white sun below.
Its constitution gives step-by-step geometric instructions for drawing it.
south-africa: A green horizontal Y separates red and blue bands, with a black triangle at the hoist.
Six colours, no emblem, designed by a state herald in a matter of weeks.
First raised on the day of its country's first fully democratic election.
It replaced an orange-white-blue flag carrying three miniature flags.
united-kingdom: Three national crosses, one upright and two diagonal, overlaid on a blue field.
It has a correct way up because its diagonal crosses are offset.
One constituent country is not represented on it at all.
It sits in the canton of several other national flags in Oceania.
united-states: Thirteen horizontal stripes of red and white and a blue canton full of white stars.
Its canton has been redesigned more than twenty times, a new version each time the federation grew.
A star is added on the Fourth of July after a new member joins.
A version with fifteen stripes inspired a national anthem written during a bombardment in 1814.
